explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. David says they will "shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces…" (Psalm 7:2). A lion is a scary picture, and he stacks the two together so we feel how serious it is. That's why he runs straight to the LORD for refuge.

I see why that sounds right, baker. David's pursuers are after him, so running him off feels natural. But the psalm never mentions driving him from the land. It says they will "shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces…" (Psalm 7:2). Tear him to pieces is the answer.

Wandering is a good guess, friend, but David doesn't say it here. His words are much sharper. He says they will "shred my soul like a lion and tear me to pieces…" (Psalm 7:2). Nobody in this verse is leaving him to stroll anywhere.

Careful, baker, this one flips it. David says the opposite: his pursuers will tear him to pieces "with no one to rescue me" (Psalm 7:2). That's exactly why he cries out to the LORD. He knows who his help has to be.

Right, friend. David says they will tear him to pieces "with no one to rescue me" (Psalm 7:2). Nobody else is coming in this picture. That's why he takes refuge in the LORD his God in the first place.

Yes, baker. David says, "if I have rewarded my ally with evil…" (Psalm 7:4). He's checking his own record out loud, and he even includes how he treated his friends. That is a man who wants the whole record read, not just the flattering parts.

It's actually on the list, friend. David says, "if I have rewarded my ally with evil…" (Psalm 7:4). He also adds plundering his foe without cause. He doesn't skip a single line when he checks himself.

explanations.answer: Let his enemy trample him down
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. David says, "then may my enemy pursue me and overtake me; may he trample me to the ground and leave my honor in the dust." (Psalm 7:5). He's that sure of himself that he names his own penalty. Not many of us would sign that paper.

explanations.answer: Let the LORD forgive him anyway
explanations.explanation: Good heart, baker, but that's not what David says. He says that if he's done these things, "may my enemy pursue me and overtake me; may he trample me to the ground and leave my honor in the dust." (Psalm 7:5). He's not asking to be let off the hook. He's showing how sure he is.

explanations.answer: Let the elders settle the matter
explanations.explanation: Interesting pick, friend, but the elders never show up in this psalm. David names the penalty himself. He says, "may my enemy pursue me and overtake me; may he trample me to the ground…" (Psalm 7:5). He lays it all before the LORD.

Yes, baker. David cries, "Awake, my God, and ordain judgment." (Psalm 7:6). He wants God to set things right. I think he's calling out because his enemies are in a fury and he has nowhere else to turn.
Peace would be nice, baker, but that's not the request. David says, "Awake, my God, and ordain judgment." (Psalm 7:6). He is asking God to judge, because the fury of his enemies is rising.
Rest sounds lovely, friend. I could use some myself. But David doesn't ask for it here. He says, "Awake, my God, and ordain judgment." (Psalm 7:6).
Not quite, baker. David doesn't bring up his crown at all. He says, "vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity." (Psalm 7:8). He's not waving rank around.

Right, baker. David asks, "vindicate me, O LORD, according to my righteousness and integrity." (Psalm 7:8). No royal rank is mentioned in that ask. Even a king stands in the same line as everybody else before the LORD.
That's right, baker. David calls Him the "righteous God who searches hearts and minds." (Psalm 7:9). He's not just checking what we do. He's looking at what's inside, too.
Good guess, baker, but paperwork isn't what David names. He says "O righteous God who searches hearts and minds." (Psalm 7:9). God looks a lot deeper than any file.
That one sounds like a land survey, friend. David says something deeper: "O righteous God who searches hearts and minds." (Psalm 7:9). So it's hearts and minds.
Yes, baker. David says, "My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart." (Psalm 7:10). When the pressure is on, that's who he points to. A shield is only as good as the One holding it.

Close to David's world, friend, but not here. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's friend (1 Samuel 18:3), isn't named in this verse. David says, "My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart." (Psalm 7:10).
Joab was David's army commander (2 Samuel 8:16), so I get the guess, baker. But David doesn't name any soldier here. He says, "My shield is with God, who saves the upright in heart." (Psalm 7:10).
Not quite, baker. David says, "God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day." (Psalm 7:11). Each day, not once in a while. That's what the verse says.

Right, friend. David says, "God is a righteous judge and a God who feels indignation each day." (Psalm 7:11). It's each day, not once in a while. He says it right alongside calling God a righteous judge.
Yes, baker. David says, "If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword…" (Psalm 7:12). The if is right there in the verse. Repenting is the door that's left open.

I see the thinking, baker, but David never says that. The verse says, "If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword…" (Psalm 7:12). Repenting is the whole point there, not whether David gets teased.
That sounds big and dramatic, friend, but it's not in this verse. David says, "If one does not repent, God will sharpen His sword…" (Psalm 7:12). The case he names is not repenting.
That's right, baker. David says, "He has prepared His deadly weapons; He ordains His arrows with fire." (Psalm 7:13). It goes with the bow he just mentioned, strung and ready.
Spears fit the battle picture, friend, but they aren't in this line. David says, "He ordains His arrows with fire." (Psalm 7:13). That goes right along with the bow in the verse before.
A shield is a good thing for David to mention, baker, and he does, but earlier in verse 10. This line is about weapons. He says, "He ordains His arrows with fire." (Psalm 7:13).
Yes, baker. David says the wicked man "conceives trouble and births falsehood." (Psalm 7:14). The trouble doesn't stay small. It grows, and out it comes.
That's a nice guess, baker, but the picture goes further. David says he "conceives trouble and births falsehood." (Psalm 7:14). It gets born, and that's the opposite of staying hidden.
That would be a gentle ending, friend, but David doesn't say that. He says the wicked man "conceives trouble and births falsehood." (Psalm 7:14). It doesn't fade. It arrives.
Yes, baker. David says, "he has fallen into a pit of his own making." (Psalm 7:15). The man digs it and then lands in it himself. That's one expensive project.
Look again, friend. David says the wicked man "has dug a hole and hollowed it out; he has fallen into a pit of his own making." (Psalm 7:15). He falls in. His own work catches him.
Yes, baker. David says, "I will thank the LORD for His righteousness…" (Psalm 7:17). After all those sharp pictures, he lands on thanks. That's a good place to land.

Patience is a nice word, baker, but David uses a different one. He says, "I will thank the LORD for His righteousness…" (Psalm 7:17). It's the same word he's been using about God all through the psalm.
I wish, friend. My drawer days never had any riches either. David says, "I will thank the LORD for His righteousness…" (Psalm 7:17). That's what he's thankful for.
